title: Dead to sin (Romans 6)
hook: baptism as burial and rising: walk in newness of life

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was charis, grace, on Paul's seesaw of Adam and Christ. Your line was grace abounds.

A kid has just been told: whatever you break, it's already forgiven. For a moment the kid looks thoughtful. Then the kid looks at the china cabinet. Paul saw this coming. He's just said that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound, and he can hear someone at the back raising a hand. If more sin means more grace, shouldn't we sin more? Maybe some people in Rome were really asking it. Paul answers with two words, then with a picture of water, a grave and a morning.
screen: `WHATEVER YOU BREAK IS FORGIVEN.` → `SO SHOULD WE SIN MORE?` → `WATER, A GRAVE, A MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the question, in the King James Bible: "What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." In Greek, me genoito: absolutely not, may it never be. Then baptism. Baptizo means to dip, to plunge under, and Paul says going under the water is like going into a grave: "Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life." The old life, run by sin, has been buried. You walk out into a new morning. Dead to sin, for Paul, doesn't mean temptation disappears; it means sin no longer owns you. He talks about slavery, a picture his hearers in Rome saw every day: you used to belong to one master, now you belong to another. And he ends the chapter: "For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord." Wages are earned. A gift is not. Churches differ. Catholics, Orthodox Christians, and Protestant churches such as Lutherans, Anglicans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize babies as well as adults, trusting God's grace comes first. Baptists, Pentecostals and others baptize only those old enough to confess faith themselves. Some pour water, some plunge the whole body under, and the Orthodox immerse even infants three times. Romans 6 is often read at baptisms, because the picture is the same: down into the water, up into new life.
screen: `SHALL WE CONTINUE IN SIN? GOD FORBID.` · `BAPTIZO: PLUNGED UNDER.` · `BURIED WITH HIM, RAISED TO WALK.` · `WAGES EARNED, A GIFT GIVEN.` · then, large: `WALK IN NEWNESS OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing from an old way of living you'd like to leave behind, like scrolling the minute you wake up or a sharp tone with someone at home, and picture it going under, like the water in Paul's picture. Then picture one small, new thing you'd do instead, tiny enough to actually start, and see yourself doing it tomorrow morning. If you pray, ask for help to walk in it.
Baptizo. The Greek word for baptism: to dip, to plunge under, like going down into a grave and walking out new.
Your line: newness of life. The grave is for leaving, not for living in. Day three hundred eighteen, done.

howItsDone: Romans 6:3–11 is often read at baptisms and at the Easter Vigil, and some Christians touch water on entering church, or recall their baptism each morning, as a reminder of dying and rising with Christ.

fork.reveal: "God forbid." Paul answers with baptism: buried with him into death, raised to "walk in newness of life."

original.note: Greek: newness of life. kainos means new in kind, not just recent.

trapdoor: what you thought: dead to sin means never being tempted.
what it means: in baptism, Paul says, the old life is buried with Christ, so sin no longer owns you, and you walk in newness of life.
what a scholar hears: early Christian baptism was often full immersion, which makes Paul's burial picture vivid, and the Greek wages, opsōnia, was a soldier's pay.

notes: Summary of baptismal practice (infant vs. believer's baptism; pouring vs. immersion; Orthodox triple immersion of infants) is compressed; confirm fair to each church.
'Early Christian baptism was often full immersion' (trapdoor): the Didache allows pouring when water is scarce; 'often' is deliberate. Confirm.
Opsōnia (wages) as a soldier's ration or pay: standard lexical sense; confirm.
Slavery metaphor (Romans 6:16–22) is mentioned briefly as a picture Paul's hearers knew 'all too well'; Keeper may want more care here.
Kainos vs. neos ('new in kind' vs. 'recent') is a common distinction that some lexicographers think is overdrawn in the New Testament; confirm the original note.
